channel.title: PsyDigest — psychiatry literature digest
channel.description: Summaries of new psychiatric research and guidelines

item.title: Comparative effectiveness of traditional Chinese medicine treatment strategies for insomnia: a systematic review and network meta-analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: Insomnia is common and impairs daytime functioning. This systematic review and network meta-analysis compared Traditional Chinese Medicine (TCM) strategies (alone or combined with Western medicine) against Western medicine, placebo, and CBT-I in randomized trials to assess efficacy and safety.
FINDINGS: Twelve RCTs (n=1,260) were included. For ISI, TCM+WM ranked highest (SUCRA 89.7%) and outperformed placebo (OR 2.84, 95% CI 1.42–5.68) and WM alone (OR 1.96, 95% CI 1.08–3.56). For PSQI, TCM+WM showed the largest reduction versus placebo (MD −2.31, 95% CI −3.65 to −0.97). Clinical efficacy favored TCM+WM (SUCRA 86.6%) over TCM (77.2%), WM (20.9%), and placebo (15.3%). Adverse events were least frequent with WM alone (SUCRA 94.8%) and more common with TCM+WM (43.9%).
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is small (12 RCTs, 1,260 participants) and heterogeneous in interventions and comparators. Network meta-analysis ranking methods are indirect and model-dependent; effect sizes are modest (e.g., PSQI MD −2.31) and may not translate to clinically meaningful differences in routine care. Safety data suggest TCM+WM may increase adverse events compared with WM alone. Overall certainty is low due to risk of bias, limited long-term follow-up, and unclear blinding in many trials.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not justify routine use of TCM+WM over established first-line treatments like CBT-I or approved pharmacotherapies. Clinicians should remain cautious about integrating TCM strategies until higher-quality, head-to-head RCTs with longer follow-up confirm efficacy and safety.

item.title: Non-pharmacological executive function interventions for children and adolescents with neurodevelopmental disorders: a systematic review and network meta-analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The review asks which non-pharmacological interventions most effectively improve executive-function outcomes in children/adolescents (5–18 y) with neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs), synthesizing randomized trials via pairwise and network meta-analysis.
FINDINGS: 118 RCTs (n=5863; 76 % male) were included; 83 focused on ADHD. Overall task-based executive function improved modestly (SMD 0.52, 95 % CI 0.45–0.60; I²=49 %). Network meta-analysis suggested computerized serious games improved cognitive flexibility (SMD 1.30, 95 % CI 0.60–2.00), working memory (SMD 0.79, 0.47–1.11) and planning (SMD 1.34, 0.44–2.24), while cognitively engaging exercise improved inhibitory control (SMD 0.65, 0.43–0.86). Most domain-specific estimates had low or very low GRADE/CINeMA confidence; Egger’s test indicated possible publication bias.
INTERPRETATION: Evidence suggests small-to-moderate benefits of non-pharmacological interventions on task-based EF, with computerized serious games and cognitively engaging exercise appearing strongest for specific domains. However, overall certainty is low due to heterogeneity, risk of bias, and publication bias, and the evidence base is dominated by ADHD samples. Results should be interpreted cautiously until larger, diagnosis-specific RCTs with standardized outcomes confirm domain-specific effects.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current findings do not justify changing first-line clinical practice, but may guide individualized adjunctive strategies (e.g., computerized cognitive training or structured physical activity) for selected EF deficits while awaiting higher-quality trials.

item.title: Effect of web-based education on NIV-related side effects and insomnia severity in COPD patients using home NIV: a randomized controlled trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study tested whether web-based education improves non-invasive ventilation (NIV)-related side effects and insomnia severity in COPD patients on home NIV, using a randomized controlled trial (RCT) with 75 participants.
FINDINGS: At weeks 4 and 8, the intervention group had significantly higher total S³-NIV Questionnaire scores (respiration, sleep, side-effects subscales) than controls. Repeated-measures ANOVA showed strong group × time interaction effects for total S³-NIV scores (p < 0.001, η²p = 0.753) and ISI scores (p < 0.001, η²p = 0.352). Insomnia severity (ISI) was not significantly different at week 4 but was lower in the intervention group at week 8.
INTERPRETATION: The RCT suggests web-based education improves patient-reported NIV-related symptoms and insomnia by week 8, with large effect sizes for NIV outcomes and moderate for insomnia. However, the insomnia effect emerged late and was not present at week 4, raising questions about durability or timing of assessment. The small sample and short follow-up limit generalisability; larger trials with longer follow-up are needed to confirm clinical benefit and sustainability.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Web-based education may be a low-cost adjunct to routine care for COPD patients on home NIV, particularly for symptom management, but insomnia benefits appear modest and delayed; routine adoption should await confirmation in larger, longer studies.

item.title: The nexus of mental health, human rights and sustainability: interdisciplinary approach.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review examines the intersection of climate change, mental health, and human rights, discussing potential pathways linking climate change to mental health outcomes and recent legal judgments that hold governments accountable for these impacts. It also proposes ways for psychiatrists to engage with sustainability and human rights in clinical practice, research, education, and policy.
FINDINGS: The paper highlights direct effects of climate change (e.g., extreme weather events) and indirect effects (e.g., displacement, food insecurity) on mental health, citing evidence of increased anxiety, depression, PTSD, and suicide risk in affected populations. It summarizes recent human rights court rulings (e.g., *Urgenda Foundation v. Netherlands*, *Neubauer v. Germany*) that recognize states' obligations to mitigate climate change due to its mental health harms. The authors advocate for psychiatrists to integrate human rights frameworks into their work, including advocating for climate policies and incorporating sustainability into mental health care.
INTERPRETATION: This is a narrative review, not an empirical study, so its conclusions are based on selected literature and legal cases rather than systematic evidence. The strength of the argument lies in its interdisciplinary perspective and call to action, but it lacks quantitative data or rigorous study design. The human rights lens is a plausible framework for engagement, but its practical implementation in psychiatry remains speculative without further empirical support. The paper does not quantify effect sizes or provide direct evidence of psychiatrists' impact on climate-related outcomes.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: While the paper raises important questions about the role of psychiatrists in climate advocacy and sustainability, it does not provide actionable clinical guidance or evidence-based interventions. Clinicians may consider integrating climate-related stressors into patient assessments (e.g., eco-anxiety) and advocating for systemic changes, but robust evidence for such practices is lacking. Further research is needed to determine whether these approaches improve mental health outcomes.

item.title: Reducing the risk of obesity, diabetes, and metabolic disorders in patients treated with antipsychotics - recommendations of the Polish Psychiatric Association Part I: risk factors and psychological interventions.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: Clinical guidelines from the Polish Psychiatric Association update recommendations on preventing obesity, diabetes, and metabolic disorders in patients with severe mental illness (schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, depression) treated with antipsychotics, where metabolic risk is ≥1.5-fold higher than in the general population. This first part focuses on risk factors and non-pharmacological interventions.
FINDINGS: The recommendations are based on expert consensus after reviewing literature and existing guidelines. Key preventive strategies include nutritional education, regular physical activity, meal planning, mindfulness, support groups, and progress monitoring. Pharmacological interventions are reserved for high-risk or established cases and are covered in a separate guideline section.
INTERPRETATION: These are consensus-based recommendations rather than empirical evidence from trials. Strengths include broad expert input and alignment with prior guidelines, but the lack of quantitative effect estimates (e.g., weight change, HbA1c reduction) and absence of a systematic review methodology limit internal validity. External validity depends on local healthcare resources and patient adherence; the suggested small, gradual lifestyle changes may improve feasibility but effectiveness in routine psychiatric care remains uncertain.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Psychiatrists should actively screen for metabolic risk and initiate non-pharmacological prevention early, emphasizing sustainable lifestyle modifications. Watch for barriers to adherence (e.g., negative symptoms, cognitive deficits) and consider referral to dietitians or physiotherapists where available.

item.title: Parental Cardiometabolic History, Family Income, and Cardiometabolic Risk in Antipsychotic-Treated Children, Adolescents, and Young Adults: A Nationwide Cohort Study.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This nationwide cohort study in Denmark examined how parental cardiometabolic adverse event (CMAE) history and family income influence the risk of CMAEs in children, adolescents, and young adults treated with antipsychotics. The study aimed to clarify whether these factors modify the cardiometabolic risk associated with antipsychotic use.
FINDINGS: The cohort included 8,488 children/adolescents and 27,326 young adults treated with antipsychotics, matched to 293,678 unexposed controls. Among children/adolescents, CMAE incidence increased with the number of affected parents (weighted incidence rate [wIR] with no affected parents: 10.7/1000 person-years; one parent: 14.0/1000 PY; both parents: 17.7/1000 PY). A similar gradient was observed in young adults (17.8–27.4/1000 PY). Antipsychotic-related CMAE risk was higher in children/adolescents (weighted incidence rate ratio [wIRR] 1.51–2.11) than in young adults (wIRR 1.46–1.55). Higher family income was associated with lower CMAE risk in both groups (children/adolescents: OR 0.92, 95% CI 0.89–0.95; young adults: OR 0.97, 95% CI 0.95–0.99).
INTERPRETATION: The study demonstrates a clear gradient in absolute CMAE risk based on parental history, with higher risk when both parents are affected. However, the relative risk increase associated with antipsychotic use was largest in those with no parental history, suggesting that antipsychotics may confer a proportionally greater risk in lower-risk individuals. The association with family income suggests socioeconomic factors play a role, though causality cannot be inferred. The study’s strengths include its large, nationwide sample and use of propensity score weighting, but residual confounding (e.g., lifestyle factors) and reliance on registry data for outcomes may limit precision. The clinical significance of the relative risk increases is modest, and the absolute risks remain low.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings support the importance of assessing both parental cardiometabolic history and socioeconomic context when prescribing antipsychotics to young patients. Enhanced monitoring and preventive strategies may be particularly warranted in children/adolescents with a family history of CMAEs or lower family income, though the absolute risk remains modest.

item.title: Trajectories of suicidal ideation and attempts across the academic year: longitudinal study of UK university students.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study examined longitudinal trajectories of suicidal ideation and attempts among 3,295 UK university students over an academic year (2021–2024), aiming to identify risk factors, changes in risk, and the relationship between ideation and attempts. It used a longitudinal cohort design with surveys in autumn and spring terms.
FINDINGS: At baseline, 45.5% reported lifetime suicidal ideation and 9.5% reported a prior suicide attempt. Among those with baseline ideation, 61.1% did not report ideation in spring, while 3.5% developed new-onset ideation. Of those with prior ideation only, 1.3% made a suicide attempt during the year, compared to 10.5% of those with a prior attempt history. Increases in depressive symptoms and rumination were associated with new attempts.
INTERPRETATION: The study provides valuable longitudinal data on suicidal trajectories in a large student cohort, with clear risk stratification based on prior history. However, reliance on self-report surveys and a single academic year follow-up may limit generalisability. The low absolute risk of attempts among those with ideation alone suggests ideation alone has limited predictive specificity, though high-risk groups (e.g., those with prior attempts or worsening depressive symptoms) warrant close monitoring.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Routine screening for suicidal ideation in students is important, but risk assessment should prioritise those with prior attempts or escalating depressive symptoms. Ongoing monitoring—not just initial screening—may be necessary to identify high-risk students during the academic year.

item.title: miR-181b-5p is Upregulated in First-Episode Drug-Naive Schizophrenia and Correlates with Symptom Severity and Cognitive Deficits: A Case-Control Study.
item.description: This study aimed to explore miR-181b-5p's diagnostic value in schizophrenia, analyze its correlations with symptoms and cognition, and evaluate biomarker-guided personalized nursing efficacy to inform early diagnosis and precision care. A total of 126 patients with first-episode, drug-naive schizophrenia and 126 age- and gender-matched healthy controls were enrolled between January 2024 and June 2025. Plasma miR-181b-5p and Early Growth Response 1 (EGR1) mRNA levels were measured by qRT-PCR, and their targeting was validated via dual-luciferase assay.

item.title: Effects of Incorporating Horses into Occupational Therapy on Adrenocortical and Sympathetic Nervous System Reactivity and Regulation in Autistic Children: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
item.description: PURPOSE: The study prospectively investigated adrenocortical and autonomic nervous system reactivity and regulation as autistic children participated in a randomized controlled trial of occupational therapy in an equine environment (OT-Equine). METHODS: Autistic children (n = 72, ages 6-11 yrs) were randomly assigned for 10 weeks to OT-Equine or clinic-based occupational therapy (OT-Clinic).

item.title: Zebrafish behavioral phenomics reveals functional subtypes of autism risk genes.
item.description: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a highly heterogeneous neurodevelopmental condition caused by many genetic mutations, each conferring modest individual risk. Despite its genetic complexity and clinical burden, no effective treatments targeting core symptoms are available. Although ASD is diagnosed as a single disorder, accumulating evidence suggests that it comprises biologically distinct subtypes, yet how genetic risk maps onto phenotypic substructure remains poorly defined.

item.title: The role of white matter microstructure in the association between childhood maltreatment and adult post-traumatic symptoms.
item.description: Childhood maltreatment (CM) is a risk factor for adult post-traumatic symptoms and white matter (WM) alterations. It remains unknown how WM microstructure is affected alongside two common military conditions, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI). Data from 299 participants (53% male, 35.69 ± 12.23 years of age) of the Injury and Traumatic Stress (INTRuST) clinical consortium was analyzed. The study included 56 individuals with PTSD (41 with comorbid mTBI), 107 with mTBI, and 136 controls (no PTSD and/or mTBI).

item.title: Separating neurodevelopmental and psychiatric services: clinical hazard?
item.description: Neurodevelopmental and psychiatric disorders differ in onset and course but comorbidity between groupings is high. Diagnostically siloed services risk fragmented care, misdiagnosis, inefficiency and clinical risk. Such services also deskill clinicians and intensify waiting list pressures and budget competition. We propose more person-centric systems to reduce risk and improve outcomes.

item.title: Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale - a validation of the Danish translation to the English version.
item.description: INTRODUCTION: Catatonia is a common neuropsychiatric syndrome comprising motor, behavioural, and affective symptoms. Catatonia is frequently underdiagnosed and may cause serious harm. A knowledge gap in recognising catatonia symptoms among clinicians has previously been demonstrated. The Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale (BFCRS) is the most widely used catatonia scale; it has strong inter-rater reliability and is easy to apply. No catatonia scale exists in Danish, and the aim of this study was to validate a Danish translation of the BFCRS.

item.title: Putting equity first: reorienting artificial intelligence for population-level postpartum depression prevention.
item.description: Postpartum depression (PPD) affects 10-20% of new mothers globally, yet detection and treatment rates remain low, particularly in underserved populations. Artificial intelligence (AI)-here spanning supervised machine-learning prediction, natural-language and acoustic analysis, and generative conversational agents-is increasingly promoted as a solution, from risk prediction to chatbot-delivered therapy.

item.title: Managing 7-Hydroxymitragynine Use Disorder with Buprenorphine-Naloxone.
item.description: Kratom, a plant native to Southeast Asia, is legal in Hawai'i and is used for many purposes including pain relief and opioid withdrawal. Kratom contains many alkaloids with mitragynine being the most abundant. 7-hydroxymitragynine, one of the minor alkaloids in kratom, is approximately 46 times more potent than mitragynine. In recent years, 7-hydroxymitragynine has been available online and in Hawai'i vape shops where any individual can purchase it.

item.title: Change in the life expectancy gap among people with mental illness: a 14-year population-based cohort study in Australia.
item.description: BACKGROUND: People with psychiatric disorders die substantially earlier than the general population, with life expectancy gaps of 10-20 years reported internationally. Prior Australian data indicated this gap was widening, whereas evidence from other countries has been mixed. We aimed to determine whether the life expectancy gap in people with hospitalised psychiatric disorders versus the general population is changing in Queensland, Australia, and to identify which causes of death drive excess mortality.

item.title: EEG Microstates are Not Associated with Psychotic Symptoms, Neurocognitive Domains or Psychosocial Functioning in Adolescents and Young Adults with Clinical High Risk for Psychosis.
item.description: EEG microstates are brief and discrete topographic patterns of electrical brain activity. Microstates last for 60-120 milliseconds, are thought to represent transient, quasi-stable neural networks, and traditionally four distinct classes (A-D) are distinguished. One of the core concepts of present neuroscience is that neuroimaging is able to capture meaningful networks of brain activity, which can be translated into specific cognitive functions. Following this idea, each microstate might correspond to specific core brain functions.

item.title: [Not Available].
item.description: OBJETIVO: a pesar de ser un fármaco altamente eficaz para el tratamiento de la esquizofrenia resistente al tratamiento (ERT), la clozapina continúa siendo subutilizada. Este estudio tiene como objetivo evaluar los patrones de prescripción de Clozapina en pacientes ambulatorios de un hospital especializado en psiquiatría de Argentina. Métodos: este estudio observacional descriptivo retrospectivo de corte transversal incluyó pacientes adultos con diagnóstico de esquizofrenia que realizan tratamiento ambulatorio en nuestra institución.

item.title: [Not Available].
item.description: La depresión psicótica (DP) es una manifestación grave de la depresión mayor que se caracteriza por la presencia de síntomas psicóticos, como alucinaciones y delirios, junto con los signos y síntomas típicos de la depresión. Este trastorno presenta desafíos significativos tanto en el diagnóstico como en el tratamiento debido a la complejidad de sus manifestaciones clínicas.

item.title: Twenty-year trajectories of negative symptoms following first hospitalization for schizophrenia: A Bayesian analysis.
item.description: OBJECTIVES: The aim of the study was to investigate whether three negative symptoms of schizophrenia - motor retardation, emotional withdrawal, and blunted affect - differ in their course over 20 years following first hospitalization. METHODS: Data from 80 patients in the Cracow Prospective Study of Schizophrenia, assessed at six time points over 20 years using the Brief Psychiatric Rating Scale, were reanalyzed with Bayesian cumulative ordinal multilevel models following the WAMBS (When to Worry and How to Avoid the Misuse of Bayesian Statistics) checklist.

item.title: Reconsidering the health-related burden of mental and physical disorders in the presence of comorbidity: evidence from China Mental Health Survey.
item.description: AIMS: Mental and physical disorders are leading contributors to global disability. However, estimates of their health-related burden often overlook the pervasive comorbidity among conditions. This study aimed to quantify the independent and combined effects of these disorders on self-rated health in nationally representative Chinese adults, explicitly accounting for comorbidity. METHODS: Data were drawn from the China Mental Health Survey (CMHS), a cross-sectional nationally representative survey.

item.title: Sex differences in responses to neurosteroid therapy after preterm birth.
item.description: Progesterone production by the placenta leads to elevated levels of neurosteroids in both the maternal and fetal circulations during late gestation. Allopregnanolone levels are crucial because they provide both neuroprotective and trophic support in the fetal brain. These include protecting against excessive excitation and supporting oligodendrocyte development and myelination. Pregnancy compromises and particularly premature birth reduce or totally deprive the newborn brain of this neurosteroid mediated protection and support.

item.title: Alignment with sex-typical brain architecture: Links to mood pathology, sex hormones and transcriptomics of neurodegenerative conditions.
item.description: Understanding the mechanisms that underpin the pervasive sex bias in risk for specific psychiatric and neurodegenerative conditions could substantially advance efforts promoting personalized medicine. As a first step towards addressing this issue, we applied imaging transcriptomics and multivariate analysis techniques to data from an adolescent sample enriched in anxiety/depression cases, a child sample enriched in attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) cases, and adult patients with treatment resistant major depressive disorder (MDD).

item.title: Gut Microbiota Composition in Helicobacter pylori-Positive Adolescents With Autism Spectrum Disorder: An Exploratory Compositional Analysis.
item.description: Alterations in the gut microbiota have been implicated in autism spectrum disorder (ASD), but reported microbial profiles remain inconsistent, potentially because of heterogeneity in factors affecting gut microbial composition. Because Helicobacter pylori infection is associated with alterations in the gut microbiota, we investigated whether ASD was associated with gut microbial composition in a cohort of H. pylori-positive adolescents. This cross-sectional study included seven adolescents with ASD and 80 controls before H. pylori eradication therapy.

item.title: Gut microbiota and the gut-brain axis in autism spectrum disorder and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: A scoping review of shared and disorder-specific mechanistic pathways.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) are among the most prevalent neurodevelopmental conditions worldwide, yet the biological mechanisms driving their onset and phenotypic variability remain incompletely understood.

item.title: Personality, dopamine, and addiction: the DRD4 Ex3 (VNTR) polymorphism and personality traits in men addicted to gambling and amphetamine.
item.description: OBJECTIVES: The present study analyzed the polymorphism of the dopamine receptor gene DRD4, which is widely described in the literature as being associated with sensation seeking. Gambling disorder (GD) shares similar biological mechanisms and symptoms with substance use disorders (SUD). Therefore, a behavioral addiction group was selected for this study. During the research and recruitment process, it was revealed that all individuals undergoing treatment for gambling addiction were also addicted to amphetamine, which aligns with the biological mechanism related to brain neurotransmission.

item.title: Neurophysiological Correlates of Target-Related Visual Attention Processes as a Function of Reward in Connection with Schizotypy.
item.description: In everyday life, we constantly select and perceive relevant information while suppressing irrelevant sensory input. This selection process is governed by the interaction between bottom-up and top-down attention mechanisms. Recent studies also highlighted the influence of reward on attention, with monetary rewards shown to enhance task performance and modulate stimulus salience. Schizotypy, conceptualized as a continuum ranging from healthy states to schizophrenia symptoms, provides a framework for the investigation of these mechanisms in non-clinical populations.

item.title: From Mechanistic Evidence to Clinical Translation: A Narrative Review of Chinese Herbal Medicine for Insomnia.
item.description: Insomnia is one of the most common sleep disorders and a major public health problem worldwide. Chinese herbal medicine (CHM) is widely used as a complementary and alternative approach for chronic insomnia. Clinical studies have reported preliminary evidence of benefit for Chinese herbal formulas, whereas mechanistic research has examined single herbs, extracts, active constituents, and compound formulas using multi-omics analysis, network pharmacology, molecular prediction, and experimental validation.

item.title: Connectivity-Guided Individualized iTBS of the Posterior Parietal Cortex in Enduring Anorexia Nervosa: Network-Level Target Engagement and Multimodal Response in a Single Case.
item.description: AIMS: Anorexia nervosa (AN) is a severe, often enduring disorder with scarce biological treatments, largely unable to address its core implicit features: habit-like food restriction and body-experience disturbances. We report a single-case application of resting-state connectivity-guided intermittent theta-burst stimulation (iTBS) to the posterior parietal cortex (PPC), a hub for body representation, peripersonal space, and affordance-based action.

item.title: Dropout from individual cognitive behavioral psychotherapy for schizophrenia: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized clinical trials.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis examined dropout rates from individual cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) for schizophrenia spectrum disorders (SSDs) in randomized clinical trials (RCTs), addressing a key barrier to treatment effectiveness in outpatient settings.
FINDINGS: Across 13 RCTs (16 CBT arms, n=865), the pooled dropout rate was ~20% (one in five participants). Substantial heterogeneity was observed between arms. Exploratory meta-regression found no significant associations with sociodemographic, clinical, or treatment-related moderators due to limited power.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is moderate in strength (systematic review of RCTs) but limited by heterogeneity and underpowered moderator analyses. The 20% dropout rate is clinically meaningful, but causal factors remain uncertain. The lack of significant moderators likely reflects insufficient data rather than true absence of effect.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should anticipate ~20% dropout in individual CBT for SSDs and monitor engagement closely. Current evidence does not support tailoring CBT based on the explored moderators. Further research is needed to identify predictors of dropout and strategies to reduce it.

item.title: Non-pharmacological interventions for perinatal parental depression and anxiety: a systematic review and network meta-analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The review asks which non-pharmacological interventions delivered to both parents during the perinatal period are most effective for reducing depression and anxiety in either parent. It is a systematic review and Bayesian network meta-analysis of 36 RCTs (n = 15 477 parents).
FINDINGS: For depression, multicomponent interventions showed a standardised mean difference (SMD) of –0.34 (95% credible interval [CrI] –0.60 to –0.08) and psychosocial interventions –0.25 (95% CrI –0.43 to –0.07). For anxiety, multicomponent interventions had SMD –0.48 (95% CrI –0.66 to –0.29) and parent–child interaction interventions –0.19 (95% CrI –0.36 to –0.03). Evidence certainty was rated low to moderate.
INTERPRETATION: The networks were sparse, most comparisons were indirect, heterogeneity was substantial, and the overall certainty of evidence was low to moderate. Therefore, the ranking should be regarded as provisional. Larger, head-to-head RCTs are needed before firm recommendations can be made.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence tentatively favours multicomponent family-centred programmes for perinatal parental depression and anxiety, but the small effect sizes and low certainty mean routine practice should await more robust trials.

item.title: Effect of Digital Technology-Based Interventions on Core Symptoms and Cognitive Function in Children With Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis evaluated whether digital technology-based interventions (computer-based training, serious video games, exergames, virtual reality) improve core ADHD symptoms and cognitive function in children, addressing uncertainty about their efficacy and generalisability.
FINDINGS: Thirty-seven RCTs (n≈3,000) were pooled. Digital interventions significantly reduced core symptoms (SMD −0.31, 95 % CI −0.48 to −0.14; P=.02) and improved cognition (SMD −0.33, 95 % CI −0.51 to −0.15; P=.04). Effects were strongest for serious video games on core symptoms and for computer-based training on cognition. Subgroup analyses suggested larger benefits in children <10 years and with ≤8 weeks of intervention.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is moderate-sized but heterogeneous (I² ≈60–70 %). Risk of bias was generally low to moderate; publication bias could not be ruled out. Effect sizes are modest and likely below commonly accepted thresholds for clinically meaningful change in routine care. The findings are sensitive to intervention type, age, and duration, limiting generalisability.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Digital interventions may offer small adjunctive benefits, particularly for younger children or short courses, but are not yet a replacement for established treatments. Clinicians should set realistic expectations and monitor outcomes individually.

item.title: PROMATER: protocol for a randomized controlled trial of a digital self-guided intervention to promote perinatal mental health and reduce self-criticism.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: Perinatal mental health is a public health priority, with self-criticism as a transdiagnostic vulnerability and self-compassion a protective factor. This Brazilian RCT protocol (PROMATER) tests a 3-week digital self-guided intervention targeting these processes in 130 pregnant women (28–34 weeks gestation), using an active control to isolate specific effects.
FINDINGS: The trial randomizes participants 1:1 to PROMATER (6 modules on self-compassion/mindfulness) or an active control (same structure without transdiagnostic modules). Primary outcomes are the Compassionate Self-Responding (CSR) and Uncompassionate Self-Responding (USR) scores from the Self-Compassion Scale, assessed at baseline, post-intervention, and 3-month postpartum. Secondary outcomes include depression, anxiety, quality of life, social support, and mother-infant bonding. Analysis will use Linear Mixed Models (ITT principle).
INTERPRETATION: As a protocol, no results are available yet. The design is robust (randomization, blinding of participants/data analysts, active control, ITT analysis), but external validity hinges on recruitment feasibility and adherence in routine care. The incremental benefit of targeting self-criticism/self-compassion over psychoeducation alone remains unproven until outcomes are reported. If effective, the brief, scalable digital format could address access gaps in Brazil.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: No clinical change yet—await trial outcomes. If positive, PROMATER could offer a low-cost, accessible adjunct to perinatal mental health care, but implementation would require integration into existing services and evaluation of real-world effectiveness.

item.title: Exploring the Neural Mechanisms of Acupuncture Stimulation in Autism Spectrum Disorder: Protocol for a Randomized, Sham-Controlled, Multimodal Neuroimaging Trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This is a protocol for a randomized, sham-controlled neuroimaging trial (2×2 design) aiming to explore acute neural mechanisms of acupuncture in 70 participants (35 with ASD, 35 typically developing controls) using functional near-infrared spectroscopy and electroencephalography. The study addresses whether acupuncture modulates resting-state network metrics and frontal band power differently in ASD versus controls.
FINDINGS: The trial is ongoing; to date, 23 ASD and 21 controls have been enrolled. Primary outcomes will compare resting-state network metrics and relative band power in frontal areas by diagnosis and intervention (verum vs sham). Secondary outcomes will assess group × intervention interactions on these neural markers.
INTERPRETATION: This is a well-designed, sham-controlled protocol with clear stratification and multimodal neuroimaging, which strengthens internal validity. However, as a protocol paper, no results are available yet; thus, efficacy and effect sizes remain unknown. The small sample size and exploratory nature limit power to detect meaningful clinical effects. The study may clarify acute neural correlates of acupuncture but cannot yet inform clinical practice.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: At present, this study does not change clinical practice. It may lay groundwork for future trials but should not influence decisions about acupuncture use in ASD until efficacy and safety are demonstrated in adequately powered, peer-reviewed studies.

item.title: Multidimensional Evaluation of the Efficacy of a Comprehensive Ayurveda Approach as an Add-On to Conventional Therapy in Children With Autism Spectrum Disorder: Protocol for a Randomized, Open-Label, Parallel-Group, Active-Controlled Clinical Trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This is a protocol for a randomized, open-label, parallel-group, active-controlled clinical trial (n≈80) in children aged 6–15 years with DSM-5–defined autism spectrum disorder (ASD) at a single Indian centre. It aims to test whether adding two Ayurvedic formulations (Saraswata Ghrita and Ayush Manas) to conventional therapy improves behavioural symptoms, cognition, adaptive functioning, parental quality of life, and exploratory inflammatory biomarkers over 6 months.
FINDINGS: The trial is ongoing; as of July 2026, 20 children had baseline data, 14 had completed 90-day follow-up, and 2 had finished the 6-month intervention. Planned analyses include repeated-measures ANOVA or Friedman tests with α=0.05. No efficacy results are yet available.
INTERPRETATION: Because this is a protocol with no published outcomes, readers should regard all conclusions as preliminary. The open-label design, single-centre recruitment, and lack of placebo control risk performance and detection bias. Biological endpoints are exploratory and not powered for definitive inference. Until peer-reviewed results appear, the clinical value of adjunctive Ayurveda in ASD remains unproven.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: At present, there is no direct evidence to change practice; clinicians should continue to rely on established behavioural and developmental interventions while awaiting the trial’s outcome.

item.title: Subcutaneous Esketamine in Adolescents with Severe Depressive Episodes: A Five-Case Series.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This five-case observational series examined the feasibility, tolerability, and short-term symptom changes of adjunctive subcutaneous esketamine in adolescents (15–17 years) with severe depressive episodes and limited prior treatment response. The study aimed to describe acute tolerability and preliminary efficacy signals in a real-world specialized outpatient setting.
FINDINGS: All five patients completed the eight once-weekly sessions (0.5–1.0 mg/kg). MADRS trajectories were heterogeneous: one remission, three partial improvements, and one no sustained benefit. MADRS Item 10 (suicidal ideation) decreased in four patients, and MADRS Item 8 (anhedonia) decreased in four. Transient mild dissociative symptoms and blood pressure elevations occurred in one and some patients, respectively; no severe adverse events, hospitalizations, or suicide attempts were reported during the 8-week protocol.
INTERPRETATION: This uncontrolled case series suggests feasibility and short-term tolerability of subcutaneous esketamine in adolescents under close monitoring, but the uncontrolled design, small sample, and heterogeneous outcomes preclude causal inference. The observed reductions in suicidal ideation and anhedonia-related symptoms are preliminary and should be regarded as hypothesis-generating. Larger, controlled pediatric trials with standardized dosing, suicide-specific assessments, and longer follow-up are required to establish efficacy, safety, and durability of effect.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not support routine use of subcutaneous esketamine in adolescents; it should remain investigational pending robust trials. Clinicians considering off-label use must weigh unproven benefits against uncertain long-term risks and ensure close monitoring for adverse effects.

item.title: Rethinking treatment motivation in addiction care: executive functions and personality over clinical severity- a cross-sectional study.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This cross-sectional study examined whether treatment motivation in individuals with alcohol or substance use disorders (n=190, inpatient at ADATC, April–August 2025) is better predicted by executive functions and personality traits than by clinical severity indicators.
FINDINGS: Addiction severity did not significantly predict treatment motivation (β not reported). Executive functions—especially goal-directedness—were the strongest predictors (β and effect size not provided). Personality traits showed that higher neuroticism and extraversion were associated with greater motivation, while higher psychoticism was linked to lower motivation (correlations not quantified).
INTERPRETATION: The study’s cross-sectional design precludes causal inference. The lack of effect sizes and confidence intervals limits assessment of clinical significance. Confounding by unmeasured variables (e.g., concurrent psychosocial interventions) is possible. The findings suggest cognitive and personality factors may shape motivation, but replication with longitudinal data and clearer quantification is needed before practice changes.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not justify altering routine assessment or treatment based solely on these preliminary associations; further research is required to determine whether targeting executive functions or personality traits improves motivation and outcomes in addiction care.

item.title: Associations between month/season of birth and health outcomes: an umbrella review of systematic reviews and meta-analyses.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This umbrella review synthesised systematic reviews and meta-analyses to assess whether month or season of birth is associated with long-term health outcomes, focusing on objectively measured conditions and grading the strength of evidence. It included 10 meta-analyses covering 614 pairwise associations across diverse health outcomes.
FINDINGS: Among 45 statistically significant associations, only one reached class II evidence: a modest increase in schizophrenia risk for January births (OR 1.05). Winter births were consistently linked to higher schizophrenia risk, while spring births showed associations with multiple sclerosis. Most other associations (autoimmune, oncological, perinatal) were graded as weak (class III–IV) due to small effect sizes or high heterogeneity.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is broad but largely weak; only schizophrenia shows a modest, relatively consistent signal. Methodological quality varied, and many associations reflect small effects with substantial heterogeneity or bias risk. The grading framework helps distinguish plausible signals from spurious findings, but causal inference remains uncertain.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current findings do not support using birth month/season to guide individual risk assessment or prevention strategies. Clinicians should remain aware that any observed associations are small and not clinically actionable at present.

item.title: A Primary Care E-Health Family Intervention for Risk Behaviors in Hispanic Youths: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
item.description: IMPORTANCE: Culturally tailored, evidence-based family interventions that can be effectively delivered within pediatric primary care settings may provide a scalable approach for preventing risk behaviors among Hispanic adolescents. OBJECTIVE: To evaluate whether the online eHealth Familias Unidas Primary Care (eHealth FUPC) program reduced drug use and increased condom use in Hispanic youth and to examine family functioning as a mediator.

item.title: Paracetamol overdose: systematic review of case reports and national toxicological data (2018-2023).
item.description: OBJECTIVES: Paracetamol is widely used as an analgesic and antipyretic, but its accessibility also makes it a frequent drug in overdose cases. Increasing rates of intentional paracetamol poisoning, particularly among adolescents, raise public health concerns. This study aimed to examine recent patterns of paracetamol overdose and identify risk groups for intentional self-poisoning. METHODS: A systematic review of published case reports (2018-2023) describing paracetamol overdose was conducted using PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library.

item.title: Advantage of cerebellar intermittent theta-burst stimulation in Alzheimer's disease (ACT-AD): study protocol for a multicenter, randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial.
item.description: INTRODUCTION: The cerebellum plays a crucial role in cognitive processing and thus presents a promising therapeutic target for Alzheimer's disease (AD). This trial aims to evaluate the efficacy and safety of long-term, neuronavigated cerebellar intermittent theta burst stimulation (iTBS) in patients with AD. METHODS AND ANALYSIS: The ACT-AD trial is a multicenter, randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled study involving 100 participants with mild-to-moderate AD across 4 centers in China.

item.title: Predictors of improvement in personal recovery and activity engagement among mental health service users following a group-based sensory modulation intervention.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Mental health service users often have sensory processing difficulties affecting activity engagement and personal recovery. Since interventions targeting this area are scarce, a group-based sensory modulation intervention was developed. To determine in which settings and for whom this intervention has clinical value, this study aimed to investigate whether sociodemographic and clinical baseline characteristics were associated with improvement in personal recovery and activity engagement.

item.title: White matter signatures of addiction diverge across opioids, cannabis and nicotine and predict impulsive choice in cannabis dependence.
item.description: White matter (WM) microstructure is implicated in the neurobiology of substance use disorders (SUDs), yet direct comparisons across substance-dependence syndromes remain scarce. It is also unclear whether WM abnormalities relate to impulsive decision-making and substance use severity.

item.title: Mapping the psychosis spectrum - imaging neurosubtypes from multiscale functional network connectivity.
item.description: Psychosis exhibits marked neurobiological heterogeneity that is not adequately captured by symptom-based diagnoses. Although prior efforts have identified subgroups, it remains unclear how latent disease variability manifests within the brain's multiscale intrinsic functional organization and whether these patterns can be leveraged to systematically identify biologically driven subtypes of psychosis.

item.title: The genetic orchestra of autism and its intersections with epilepsy, intellectual disability, and ADHD.
item.description: Autism is a complex condition with marked phenotypic variability and a multifactorial etiology orchestrated by diverse genetic and environmental influences. In this review, we dissect what we refer to as autism's "genetic orchestra", spanning from the high-impact "soloists", de novo and ultra-rare variants with large effect sizes, to the "polyphonic background" of common variants which individually exert modest effects but collectively have significant impact.

item.title: Childhood Trauma, Recent Stressors, and Risk of Depression Relapse in Late-Life Depression.
item.description: BACKGROUND: Recent stressors have been linked to poor outcomes of late-life depression (LLD), including relapse. Emerging evidence has linked adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) to the occurrence of LLD. We sought to examine the relationships between recent exposure to stressful life events and ACEs with relapse following remission among older adult. METHODS: In this cohort study, depressed older adults (age ≥65) were provided standard antidepressant medications by a study psychiatrist.

item.title: Staged bilateral reverse sural artery flap reconstruction for severe frostbite of both feet in a patient with schizophrenia: A case report.
item.description: RATIONALE: Bilateral, weight-bearing heel defects after frostbite are difficult to reconstruct, and outcomes depend heavily on postoperative off-loading and patient cooperation. We report a limb-salvage strategy for severe bilateral foot frostbite that occurred during acute psychosis in a patient diagnosed with schizophrenia. PATIENT CONCERNS: A 25-year-old man developed acute psychotic symptoms and walked barefoot in subzero conditions for about 12 hours, resulting in deep frostbite of both heels and multiple toes.

item.title: Neuronal IL-18 Signaling in the Medial Habenula Contributes to Schizophrenia-Like Behavioral Deficits via ERK-Associated BDNF Suppression.
item.description: Current antipsychotics for schizophrenia (SCZ) are notably ineffective against the debilitating cognitive and negative symptoms, creating a major therapeutic gap. Neuroinflammation in the medial habenula (MHb) is implicated in SCZ; however, the underlying cell-type-specific mechanisms remain unknown. This study aimed to determine whether pathologically elevated neuronal interleukin-18 (IL-18) in the MHb contributes to schizophrenia-like behavioral abnormalities through ERK-associated downregulation of brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF).
